Planning notes: longest chains, how the sizes were set, research

Longest chains

What has to come first to reach the big ones. The order inside each step is free.

  • The mech as a character file: Character files and the Characters tab → Attributes, effects and abilities → HUD editor → The mech as a character file
  • Goo swarm enemies: Character files and the Characters tab → Attributes, effects and abilities → Brains → Goo swarm enemies
  • Screens and menus: Character files and the Characters tab → Attributes, effects and abilities → HUD editor → Screens and menus
  • Vehicles: Character files and the Characters tab → Ways of moving and switching rules → Vehicles
  • Destructible props: Character files and the Characters tab → Attributes, effects and abilities → Health, shields and death → Destructible props

How the sizes were set

S
One small thing in one place: a new part type, a menu, a setting.
M
A system with its UI, tested in Xvfb: triggers, health, the jump family.
L
A system plus its editor and a second layer: lights, physics, abilities. 2–3 parts.
XL
New ground with several layers: the timeline, vehicles, brains, the HUD, the goo swarm. 4+ parts.

Libraries that cut the work, all checked against Bevy 0.20: avian3d (physics), vleue_navigator (navigation areas), bevy_tnua (walking), bevy_kira_audio (sound), lightyear (multiplayer).

Research behind the new areas

Idles, barks and interaction

Crowds look wrong when everyone plays the same idle: guides suggest 3–5 idle variations per character type and random offsets so footsteps don't sync. Fidgets (scratching, looking around) start after standing still a while. Head look-at is a cheap procedural layer, and hands reach handles with two-bone IK that blends in and out; holding is easy, the blend is the hard part.

NPC animation guide (MoCap Online) · One line of look-at IK (Ergastulum) · Roblox IKControl (doorknob example) · Hand IK blend weights (Unreal forum)

Driving

Arcade handling starts simple and adds mechanics until it feels right: steering limited by speed (curbs understeer), the handbrake locks the rear wheels to start a drift, clean drifts refill boost, boost is spent on the way out. Simulation adds weight transfer and counter-steering; Beverly's vehicles start arcade with those as settings.

Racing game approaches and trade-offs (Game Developer) · Need for Speed Heat handling model (EA) · Disney Speedstorm drift diary

Flying

Arcade flight keeps pitch, yaw and roll with automatic banking in turns, plus speed and lift limits. Manoeuvres become moves: aileron roll (a full roll), barrel roll (a roll with a pull, evasive), dive, loop, Immelmann (half loop and half roll: turn back, gain height), split-S (the reverse: turn back, gain speed), stall turn, boost.

Arcade-style airplane (Godot recipes) · How to Immelmann (World of Warplanes) · How to barrel roll (World of Warplanes) · How to split-S (World of Warplanes)

Moves and abilities

Platformers hide forgiveness in jumping: coyote time (jump just after leaving an edge) and jump buffering. Air dashes usually reset on landing. Dodges pair a short invulnerability with a step; parries are timed blocks. Shooters add slide, wall-run and mantle; stealth adds crouch tiers, lean, cover and hiding in shadow.

GDevelop advanced jump · Celeste and forgiveness · Defensive mechanics · Stealth game animation design

World sizes, terrain, caves

Positions are 32-bit, so worlds past about 10 km jitter; the fix is a floating origin or camera-relative maths. Heightfields can't make overhangs; games add caves with sculpted volumes (smooth add / subtract shapes turned into meshes) or hand-made pieces, and build dungeons from modular kits, often laid out by a generator. Rooms joined by portals hide what can't be seen indoors; they don't suit open ground. Beverly's terrain is described by curves and strokes, not height images.

Godot: double precision for large worlds · How terrain works (Unity) · Voxel Tools overview · Dungeon generator from a kit · Godot rooms and portals

Water

Oceans layer a few Gerstner waves: stable and easy to tune. Rivers are paths with width, depth and flow speed per point; foam drifts with the flow. Waterfalls are usually custom pieces with mist and ripple rings where they land. Buoyancy samples the water height and pushes things up with drag. In Unreal, water fought with world streaming, so Beverly's water belongs to streaming regions from the start.

GPU Gems: effective water simulation · Planet Coaster 2 water · Unreal water and World Partition

Look: post-processing, styles, wind

Bevy 0.20 already has depth of field, motion blur, bloom, chromatic aberration, vignette, lens distortion, colour grading, auto exposure, SSAO, screen-space reflections, volumetric fog, a physical sky, TAA / SMAA and GPU occlusion culling, so these are mostly editor work. Cel shading bands light into 2–5 steps; outlines are cheap shells (gaps on hard edges) or precise screen edge detection (costlier, noisier); games often mix them. One wind (direction, strength, gusts) feeds foliage sway in two layers, cloth, flags, particles and sails.

bevy_post_process · Toon outlines (Kodeco) · Cel shading · Vegetation that reacts to the environment · Zephyr wind shaders

Multiplayer

Shooters and most online games use an authoritative server: each player's own moves show at once and are corrected when the server answers. Rollback (every machine simulates and rewinds on a wrong guess) suits two-player fighting games and needs a deterministic game. Multiplayer touches characters, physics, scripting and saving, so if it's wanted it should be decided early, even if it's built late.

Authoritative servers, relays and peer-to-peer (Edgegap) · Rollback netcode explained · Unity network topologies

Space and level edges

Classic space games fly like aircraft; Newtonian flight keeps momentum, and Elite layers a switchable flight assist over it so ships stay controllable. For the edge of a level, games warn and count down (“return to the combat area”), push the player back, damage them in a hazard zone or wrap them around; developers report wrapping rarely feels good in 3D and round areas beat square ones.

Elite Dangerous flight model · Star Citizen flight model (PC Gamer) · Border Patrol (TV Tropes) · Solutions for screen wrap (Sins forum)

Risks found in the second pass

Bevy releases every 3–4 months and each library has to catch up before Beverly can move, so Beverly stays pinned and upgrades on purpose (about a session each time). Physics: one collision world, not two. Animation: Prism has no skeletons yet, so pose and key comes to Beverly. Multiplayer: a fixed time step from the start. Effects: one particle system, Last Ascent's, and the Plume Editor's files as the effect format. Rasters: decals, reflections, foliage and terrain paint are kept as math, strokes or captured at load.

lightyear (prediction, rollback, Avian) · bevy-tnua · Bevy release process

Last Ascent path · step 4

22

Physics for loose objects

L

Avian becomes the one collision world: level parts and models get colliders, moving parts are kinematic, crates and barrels tumble, characters push and stand on them, blasts shove them.

ready · Level building · needs Basic shapes, placing and the move widget ✓

Two collision worlds side by side (today's and Avian's) would need every moving part kept in step twice, so Avian replaces today's. Loose things need convex shapes (Avian builds them from the mesh); exact mesh colliders only for things that never move. avian3d 0.8 supports Bevy 0.20 and has f64 and enhanced-determinism options for big worlds and multiplayer. Part 1 built (2026-11-15): avian3d 0.8 runs while playing on a fixed 60 Hz step, drawn smoothed between steps; each Solid part becomes a body (boxes as boxes; still shapes and models exact; loose ones a hull or convex pieces); a Physics setting (Still / Loose) on parts, shared by instances; Moves parts are moving bodies; the walker moves and slides through Avian and rides moving bodies; everything goes back when play stops. Test project: tests/physics. MCP: the Physics setting on add_part and change_part. Part 2 built (2026-11-15): the walker is a bevy_tnua 0.33 character, a dynamic body floating 1.1 m up (it walks up steps of up to 0.45 m and slopes, and rides moving parts), grip and slippery feels (Slippery ground: slow to speed up and to stop); the old triangle collision (Play::world) is gone, and a game's own character collides through Avian (Play's doc comment). The user chose to rebuild Last Ascent's mech after Beverly is built instead of porting it now: notes for that are on The mech as a character file. Test project: tests/steps; the lift traces re-recorded for the new walker. MCP: get_play's velocity, ground and standing_on come from the walker's body.

22.1 · a sessionAvian as the collision world: colliders for shapes and models (box, hull, convex pieces, exact for still things), still / moving / loose parts, a fixed time step with smoothing; Moves become moving bodies; the walker moves and slides through it
22.2 · a sessionThe walker on bevy_tnua (slopes, steps, moving platforms); a game's own character collides through Avian, and the old collision code retires (Last Ascent's mech moves when it is rebuilt as a character file)
22.3 · a sessionLoose parts: mass, friction, sleeping; characters push and stand on them; impulses from blasts and the winch

Terrain from curves and strokes

XL

Terrain described as control points, curves and stroke operations (raise along a curve, flatten a pad, carve a bed, noise layers), built into meshes per chunk; no height images stored.

planned · World and maps · needs World settings · Paths tool and animating overlay

Height images from other tools could be converted into strokes later, if wanted. Collision (user, 2026-11-15: no meshes where a height function does it cheaper): the ground is the height function itself as a custom shape in Avian that answers rays exactly (standing on it: the walker's tnua sensor as a ray instead of a disc; feet and foot placement, grapple, camera, bullets, placing things), plus a small contact rule of Beverly's own, since Parry works out contact between solid shapes only for its built-in ones: each step, loose bodies' lowest points are checked against the height and pushed up and out along the slope, and ground steeper than a set limit (banks taller than the walker's 0.45 m step) pushes characters back like a wall. Check: sampled points agree with the height function, the walker climbs stairs and is stopped by a steep bank, a loose crate settles on a slope.

84

The mech as a character file

L

Last Ascent's mech rebuilt from Beverly's blocks; the extra Last Ascent editor and player retire.

planned · Characters · needs Joint chains and procedural animation · Attributes, effects and abilities · Visual effects · Character camera and controls · Jetpack and grapple · HUD editor · Physics for loose objects · Ways of moving and switching rules

Scripted tests record today's mech before anything changes, so the port can be compared step by step. What to look for when converting it (Physics part 2, 2026-11-15): Beverly no longer hands a game's character the level's triangles (Play::world, with pieces() and offsets(), is gone), so Last Ascent's own editor and player stop building once they update past this; the user chose to rebuild the mech after Beverly is built, not to port it twice. Collision is now Avian's world while playing (physics.rs): each Solid part is a body tagged PartBody(id), still ones static, Moves ones kinematic (their LinearVelocity carries what stands on them), Loose ones dynamic, plus the ground at y = 0. The mech's own physics maps onto it: its sphere-against-triangles step becomes a body of its own (a bevy_tnua character like the walker in play.rs, or Avian's MoveAndSlide), its raycast (grapple, camera, ground) Avian's SpatialQuery::cast_ray, its ground_y (the legs' foot placement) a ray down, and riding moving parts comes free. Physics runs on the fixed 60 Hz step (single precision, Avian's Gravity 9.81 with GravityScale for heavier falls): the mech's movement moves from Update with a variable step to FixedUpdate, catching one-off keys every frame as play.rs does (Play::press), and still sets Play::feet for buttons. Its recorded runs (walk, jets, grapple) will drift with the new collision: compare them, and re-record only when the user agrees.
